questions.q: What is the main advantage of k-fold cross-validation over a single train/test split?
options: It produces several scores, so you see the average and how much the score varies
It removes the need for a final held-out test set
It makes the model train faster
It guarantees the model will not overfit
questions.explain: Every fold takes a turn as the validation set, giving k scores. The mean and spread are a more stable and more honest estimate than one lucky or unlucky split.

questions.q: In 5-fold cross-validation, how many times is the model trained?
options: Once
Twice
Five times, each on four folds and scored on the fifth
Twenty-five times
questions.explain: Each of the five folds is held out once, and the model is trained on the remaining four folds each time.

questions.q: Why did the lesson use StratifiedKFold for the churn problem?
options: Because it is the only splitter that accepts a pipeline
So each fold keeps roughly the same share of churners as the whole dataset
Because it shuffles the columns of the data
Because it ignores the target variable
questions.explain: Stratification preserves the class proportions in every fold, which matters most when one class is smaller.

questions.q: Selecting the top 10 features on 100 rows of pure noise, before cross-validation, reported a score near 0.79. What went wrong?
options: The logistic regression was too simple
Five folds are too few
The feature selector saw the labels of the validation rows, so information leaked
The noise data was not shuffled
questions.explain: Feature selection used all the labels, including those of the rows later used for validation. Putting the selector inside the pipeline refits it on each training fold and gives the honest score of about 0.54.

questions.q: Which call returns several metrics per fold, and can also return training scores?
options: cross_val_score with scoring set to a list
cross_validate with a list of scorers and return_train_score=True
train_test_split with cv=5
StratifiedKFold.score()
questions.explain: cross_validate accepts a list of scoring names and, with return_train_score=True, includes train scores, so you can compare train and validation performance.
